title: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures (Chapter 5, REST)
text:
## What REST actually is
REST is defined by a set of architectural constraints applied to components, connectors, and data. A backend engineer who invokes the word REST should be able to name all six constraints and their tradeoffs, not just say 'JSON over HTTP'.

## Client-Server
Separates user interface concerns from data storage concerns. Fielding: 'By separating the user interface concerns from the data storage concerns, we improve the portability of the user interface across multiple platforms and improve scalability by simplifying the server components.'

## Stateless
'Each request from client to server must contain all of the information necessary to understand the request, and cannot take advantage of any stored context on the server. Session state is therefore kept entirely on the client.' Benefits: visibility (a monitor can understand a request from a single datum), reliability (easier recovery from partial failures), scalability (the server can quickly free resources because it stores no per-request state). Tradeoff: 'It may decrease network performance by increasing the repetitive data (per-interaction overhead) sent in a series of requests.'

## Cache
'Cache constraints require that the data within a response to a request be implicitly or explicitly labeled as cacheable or non-cacheable.' Benefit: reduce the average latency of a series of interactions. Tradeoff: 'A cache can decrease reliability if stale data within the cache differs significantly from the data that would have been obtained had the request been sent directly to the server.'

## Uniform Interface
'The central feature that distinguishes the REST architectural style from other network-based styles is its emphasis on a uniform interface between components.' It is defined by four interface constraints: identification of resources; manipulation of resources through representations; self-descriptive messages; and hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS). Tradeoff: 'A uniform interface degrades efficiency, since information is transferred in a standardized form rather than one which is specific to an application's needs.'

## Layered System
Constrains component behavior so each component cannot see beyond the immediate layer, enabling load balancing of services across multiple networks and processors. Disadvantage: layers 'add overhead and latency to the processing of data, reducing user-perceived performance.'

## Code-On-Demand (optional)
Allows client functionality to be extended by downloading and executing code in the form of applets or scripts. This is the only optional constraint.

## Resource and Representation (the core abstractions)
Resource: 'The key abstraction of information in REST is a resource. Any information that can be named can be a resource: a document or image, a temporal service (e.g. today's weather in Los Angeles), a collection of other resources, a non-virtual object (e.g. a person), and so on.' More formally, 'A resource is a conceptual mapping to a set of entities, not the entity that corresponds to the mapping at any particular point in time.' Representation: 'REST components perform actions on a resource by using a representation to capture the current or intended state of that resource and transferring that representation between components. A representation is a sequence of bytes, plus representation metadata to describe those bytes.'

title: IETF RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (safe methods, idempotent methods, status codes)
text:
## Safe methods (Section 9.2.1)
'Request methods are considered safe if their defined semantics are essentially read-only; that is, the client does not request, and does not expect, any state change on the origin server as a result of applying a safe method to a target resource.' The safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE. Safe methods let caches, crawlers, and prefetchers act without fear of side effects, so never mutate state behind a GET.

## Idempotent methods (Section 9.2.2)
'A request method is considered idempotent if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request.' The idempotent methods are GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, and TRACE. PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe (they change state, but repeating them yields the same final state). POST is neither safe nor idempotent: two identical POSTs may create two resources. This is why unsafe non-idempotent operations need an idempotency mechanism (for example an idempotency key) so a client-side retry after a timeout does not duplicate the effect.

## Status code classes (Section 15.1)
1xx (Informational): an interim response that ought not contain a message body. 2xx (Successful): 'the request was successful and the response payload typically contains the result of the request action.' 3xx (Redirection): 'further action needs to be taken to satisfy the request.' 4xx (Client Error): 'the client appears to have erred.' 5xx (Server Error): 'the server is aware that it has erred or is incapable of performing the requested method.'

## Key individual codes
200 OK: the request succeeded. 201 Created: the request succeeded and a new resource was created as a result (return a Location header for the new resource). 400 Bad Request: the server will not process the request due to a perceived client error (malformed syntax). 401 Unauthorized: the request lacks valid authentication credentials. 403 Forbidden: the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it (authenticated but not authorized). 404 Not Found: no current representation for the target resource. 409 Conflict: the request conflicts with the current state of the server (used for optimistic concurrency conflicts and uniqueness violations). 422 Unprocessable Content: the request is well-formed but contains semantic errors (validation failure). 500 Internal Server Error: an unexpected condition prevented fulfilling the request. 503 Service Unavailable: the server is temporarily unable to handle the request (overload or maintenance; pair with Retry-After). Note: 429 Too Many Requests is defined in RFC 6585, not RFC 9110; use it for rate limiting.

title: IETF RFC 9457, Problem Details for HTTP APIs
text:
## Why a standard error format
RFC 9457 (which obsoletes RFC 7807) defines a 'problem detail' to carry machine-readable details of errors in HTTP response content, 'to avoid the need to define new error response formats for HTTP APIs.' The anti-pattern it replaces: every API inventing its own ad hoc error shape, forcing every client to special-case it. A standard shape lets generic HTTP software and intermediaries handle errors and lets clients act on errors programmatically.

## The media type
JSON problem details use the media type application/problem+json (XML uses application/problem+xml). The HTTP status line still carries the real status; the problem body carries the detail.

## The standard members
type: a URI reference identifying the problem category; when absent it defaults to about:blank. Consumers must use the type URI (after resolution if necessary) as the problem type's primary identifier. status: the HTTP status code as a number, advisory only (the response status line takes precedence for generic software). title: a short human-readable summary of the problem type, stable across occurrences except for localization. detail: a human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence, ideally helping the client resolve it rather than dumping debug internals. instance: a URI reference identifying this specific occurrence, possibly dereferenceable.

## Extension members
A problem object may add custom members beyond the standard five (for example a numeric balance, a list of accounts, a validation errors array). Clients must ignore members they do not recognize so the format can evolve.

## Example
{
  "type": "https://example.com/probs/out-of-credit",
  "title": "You do not have enough credit.",
  "detail": "Your current balance is 30, but that costs 50.",
  "instance": "/account/12345/msgs/abc",
  "balance": 30,
  "accounts": ["/account/12345", "/account/67890"]
}

## Backend practice
Return problem+json for 4xx and 5xx, keep type URIs stable and documented, put a correlation id in an extension member for support, and never leak stack traces or SQL in detail. A stable type field lets clients branch on error category without string-matching human prose.

title: Google API Improvement Proposals, AIP-121 Resource-oriented design
text:
## Resource-oriented design
AIP-121 describes resource-oriented design as 'a pattern for specifying RPC APIs, based on several high-level design principles': APIs use individually-named resources (nouns) and their relationships and hierarchies as the fundamental building blocks; a limited set of standard methods (verbs) handles most operations, with custom methods available only when standard methods do not fit; and a stateless protocol where 'each interaction between the client and the server is independent.'

## Resources and collections
'A resource-oriented API should generally be modeled as a resource hierarchy, where each node is either a simple resource or a collection of resources.' A collection contains resources of the same type. Resources are named entities addressed by a resource name (a path), for example a book inside a shelf inside a library forms a hierarchy of collections and resources.

## Do not mirror your database schema
A key warning: an API surface need not, and often should not, mirror the underlying database structure. Doing so is 'actually an anti-pattern, as it tightly couples the surface to the underlying system.' The public contract should be designed for clients, not leaked from your tables.

## The five standard methods
Create (request contains the resource, response is the resource), Get (no request body, response is the resource), Update (request contains the resource, response is the resource), Delete (no request body, no response body), and List (no request body, response contains resources). Every resource must support at minimum Get, and must also support List except for singleton resources. These map to POST (create), GET (get/list), PUT or PATCH (update), and DELETE.

## Prefer standard methods over custom verbs
'APIs should prefer standard methods over custom methods.' Custom methods (like :cancel or :publish) are only for functionality that does not cleanly map to a standard method; they are expressed as a custom verb in the URI (typically over POST), not as a new HTTP method. Modeling everything as RPC-style verbs (createOrderRpc, getOrderRpc) is the anti-pattern this design replaces.

title: Markus Winand, Anatomy of an SQL Index (Use The Index, Luke)
text:
## An index is a separate data structure
Markus Winand, author of SQL Performance Explained, teaches that a database index is 'a distinct structure in the database that is built using the create index statement.' Creating an index 'does not change the table data; it just creates a new data structure that refers to the table.' The most common index type is the B-tree index.

## Two structures working together
The index is built from two cooperating structures: the index leaf nodes, organized as a doubly linked list, and a balanced search tree (the B-tree) built on top of those leaf nodes. The leaf nodes store the indexed columns plus a pointer (for example a rowid or the primary key) back to the table row.

## Why a logical order, not physical order
Databases cannot keep table rows physically sorted because rows change through insert, delete, and update. Instead the index keeps its entries 'in a well-defined order' inside the leaf nodes, independent of the physical row order in the table. Because the leaf nodes are a doubly linked list, the database can read a range of index entries forward or backward without touching the whole table.

## How a lookup works
To find a value the database does a tree traversal: it descends the balanced tree from the root through branch nodes to the correct leaf node (a logarithmic number of steps), then follows the leaf-node chain to read the matching entries in order, then uses the row pointers to fetch the actual rows from the table. The tree traversal is the fast part; excessive table access for many matching rows is where slow queries hide.

## An index is redundancy with a cost
'An index is pure redundancy': it requires its own disk space and holds a copy of the indexed table data, and every insert, delete, and index-key update must also maintain the index. So an index is never free. The engineering skill is indexing the columns queries actually filter and join on, not indexing everything.

title: Stripe API Reference, Idempotent requests
text:
## The problem idempotency keys solve
Stripe's API supports idempotency for safely retrying requests without accidentally performing the same operation twice. When creating or updating an object you send an idempotency key; then if a connection error occurs you can safely repeat the request without risk of creating a second object or performing the update twice. This is the standard cure for the classic distributed-systems trap: the request succeeded on the server but the response was lost, so a naive client retry double-charges.

## How it works
Stripe saves the resulting status code and body of the first request made for any given idempotency key, regardless of whether it succeeds or fails. Subsequent requests with the same key return the same result, including 500 errors. You send the key in the Idempotency-Key HTTP header (or IdempotencyKey request option).

## Generating keys
The client generates the idempotency key, a unique key the server uses to recognize retries of the same request. Stripe suggests V4 UUIDs or another random string with enough entropy to avoid collisions. Keys are up to 255 characters long. Avoid using sensitive data (email addresses, personal identifiers) as keys.

## Lifetime and validation
Keys are removed automatically after they are at least 24 hours old; a new request is generated if a key is reused after the original is pruned. The idempotency layer compares incoming parameters to the original request and errors if they are not the same, to prevent accidental misuse (reusing one key for two different operations). Results are saved only after the endpoint begins executing: if incoming parameters fail validation, or the request conflicts with another request executing concurrently, no idempotent result is saved and you can retry.

## Which methods
All POST requests accept idempotency keys. Do not send them on GET and DELETE, where they have no effect: those methods are idempotent by definition. The backend lesson: make unsafe, non-idempotent writes (POST) safe to retry by persisting the first outcome under a client-supplied key, ideally with a unique constraint on the key in your own datastore.

title: Markus Winand, No Offset (keyset pagination vs OFFSET) (Use The Index, Luke)
text:
## The OFFSET pagination anti-pattern
Markus Winand argues against paging with OFFSET. Two problems. First, performance: OFFSET forces the database to fetch and drop all the preceding rows before returning the page. The SQL standard says the engine must sort by the ORDER BY and then drop the number of rows specified by OFFSET, so deeper pages get slower and slower, doing more and more wasted work: page 1 is cheap, page 10000 is expensive, regardless of engine. Second, correctness under concurrent writes: if a row is inserted (or deleted) between fetching page N and page N+1, OFFSET shifts, so you can get the same row twice or skip a row entirely. Offset paging is unstable on a moving dataset.

## The seek method (keyset pagination)
The fix Winand teaches is the seek method, also called keyset pagination. Instead of an offset you remember the sort key of the last row you saw and filter on it:

SELECT ...
  FROM ...
 WHERE ...
   AND id < ?last_seen_id
 ORDER BY id DESC
 FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY

Because results stay ordered and the WHERE condition sits on an indexed column, the database can seek directly to the correct position using the index and read only the next 10 rows. There is no discard-and-recount penalty, so page 10000 is as fast as page 1, and inserts elsewhere cannot duplicate or skip rows. For composite ordering (for example created_at then id as a tiebreaker) the predicate becomes a row-value comparison like (created_at, id) < (?, ?). The tradeoff is you lose random jump-to-page-N access; you page forward and backward from a cursor, which is exactly what infinite-scroll and API cursors want anyway.

title: PostgreSQL Documentation, Using EXPLAIN
text:
## Reading a query plan
EXPLAIN shows the plan the planner chose, as a tree of plan nodes. Bottom-level nodes are scan nodes that return raw rows (Seq Scan, Index Scan, Bitmap Index Scan); upper nodes join, aggregate, and sort. Each node line ends with cost estimates in parentheses. Example:
 Seq Scan on tenk1  (cost=0.00..445.00 rows=10000 width=244)
The four numbers are: estimated start-up cost (work before the first row can be emitted, for example a sort), estimated total cost (to run the node to completion), estimated number of rows output, and estimated average row width in bytes. Cost is in an abstract unit (disk-page fetches by default), for example (345 pages x seq_page_cost 1.0) + (10000 rows x cpu_tuple_cost 0.01) = 445. Costs are cumulative: a parent node's cost includes its children.

## Node types and when the planner picks them
Seq Scan reads the whole table, chosen when most rows are needed. Index Scan (for example 'Index Scan using tenk1_unique1 ... Index Cond: (unique1 = 42)') is chosen for very selective conditions returning few rows: it costs more per row but the total is lower when few rows match. Bitmap Index Scan plus Bitmap Heap Scan sits in between for moderate selectivity. Join strategies vary with size: Nested Loop for small inputs, Hash Join for larger ones, Merge Join when inputs are already sorted.

## EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Plain EXPLAIN shows only estimates and does not run the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and adds the real numbers: actual time (ms), actual rows, and loops per node, plus Planning Time and Execution Time. Comparing estimated rows to actual rows is the single most useful debugging move: a big gap (say estimated 10 rows, actual 2,000,000) means the statistics are stale or a correlation is being missed, which is why the planner chose a bad plan; ANALYZE the table or add statistics. Watch for 'Rows Removed by Filter' (work done then thrown away) and Sort Method / Memory (a disk spill means work_mem is too small).

## Caveats the docs stress
Costs are not linear, so results on a tiny table do not extrapolate to a big one. LIMIT can make actual rows and time far below the estimate because the scan stops early. EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds measurement overhead and does not include network transmission to the client. The backend habit: never guess why a query is slow, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and read the plan.

title: PostgreSQL Documentation, Explicit Locking (row locks, pessimistic locking, deadlocks, advisory locks)
text:
## Row-level locks and pessimistic locking
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is pessimistic locking: it locks the selected rows as if for update, so other transactions cannot UPDATE, DELETE, or acquire a conflicting row lock until this transaction ends. Example: SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE acctnum = 11111 FOR UPDATE. Without it, two transactions could both read a row and both write, and one silently overwrites the other (lost update). FOR UPDATE serializes the writers on that row. There are four row lock modes from strongest to weakest: FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE. FOR SHARE is a shared read lock (many readers, no writer). FOR KEY SHARE only blocks operations that change the key, so foreign-key checks do not needlessly block ordinary updates. Row-level locks never block plain SELECT (readers); they block only writers and lockers of the same row. In REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, FOR UPDATE throws a serialization error if the row changed since the transaction started, which you retry.

## Deadlocks
A deadlock is a circular wait: transaction 1 holds row A and wants row B while transaction 2 holds row B and wants row A. PostgreSQL automatically detects deadlocks and aborts one of the transactions so the others proceed; which one is aborted is hard to predict and should not be relied on. The prevention rules: acquire locks on multiple objects in a consistent order across all code paths, acquire the strongest lock you will need up front rather than escalating, keep transactions short (never hold one open waiting for user input), and always be prepared to retry a transaction that aborts with a deadlock or serialization error.

## Advisory locks
Advisory locks are application-defined locks not tied to any row, useful for coordinating work (for example ensuring only one worker runs a job) or emulating pessimistic locking without table bloat. The system does not enforce their meaning, correctness depends on every code path agreeing to take them. They come in session level (held until released or the session ends, survive rollback) and transaction level (auto-released at transaction end). pg_try_advisory_lock is the non-blocking variant. A caveat: SELECT pg_advisory_lock(id) FROM foo WHERE id > 12345 LIMIT 100 may lock rows the LIMIT would have excluded, leaving dangling locks; wrap the row selection in a subquery first.

## Table-level locks
Every statement also takes a table lock. Only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (taken by DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL, and many ALTER TABLE forms) blocks a plain SELECT, which is why schema migrations that grab ACCESS EXCLUSIVE can stall all reads. Monitor contention with the pg_locks view.

title: Chris Richardson, Pattern: Transactional Outbox (microservices.io)
text:
## The dual write problem
A service often must atomically update its database AND publish a message or event (for example save an Order and publish OrderCreated). Doing both as two independent writes, one to the database and one to the message broker, is the 'dual write' problem: if the process crashes between them, you either committed the data but never published the event, or published an event for data that rolled back. A distributed (two-phase / 2PC) transaction spanning the database and the broker is undesirable and often unsupported. Messages must also be published in the order the service produced them.

## The solution: an outbox table plus a message relay
Richardson: 'The solution is for the service that sends the message to first store the message in the database as part of the transaction that updates the business entities. A separate process then sends the messages to the message broker.' Concretely you add an OUTBOX table. In the same local ACID transaction that updates the business rows, you also INSERT the message into the outbox. Because it is one transaction, the message is stored if and only if the business change commits. A separate component, the MESSAGE RELAY, reads unpublished rows from the outbox and publishes them to the broker, marking them sent.

## Two ways to read the outbox
Transaction log tailing: use change data capture (CDC) to tail the database transaction log and detect inserts into the outbox, streaming them to the broker (for example Debezium). Polling publisher: a background job periodically SELECTs unpublished outbox rows and publishes them. Log tailing is lower latency and lower load; polling is simpler but must be tuned and can lag.

## Consequences
'2PC is not used' and 'messages are guaranteed to be sent if and only if the database transaction commits.' The cost is at-least-once delivery: the relay can crash after publishing but before marking the row sent, so it may republish. Therefore consumers must be idempotent (deduplicate by message id or use an idempotent receiver). Richardson notes this is acceptable in practice because brokers already redeliver, so idempotent consumers are standard anyway. The outbox pattern, plus idempotent consumers, is how backends get reliable event publishing without distributed transactions or the fantasy of exactly-once delivery.

title: Chris Richardson, Pattern: Idempotent Consumer (microservices.io)
text:
## The problem
Message brokers use at-least-once delivery: they guarantee a message is delivered even across errors, and the side effect is that 'the consumer can be invoked repeatedly for the same message.' If the handler is not idempotent, duplicates cause real bugs, for example a debit consumer subtracting from an account balance twice for one payment.

## The solution
'Make a consumer idempotent by having it record the IDs of processed messages in the database.' Before (or while) processing, the consumer checks whether it has already handled that message id; if so it discards the duplicate; if not it processes and records the id, all in the same transaction as the business change so the two commit or roll back together.

## Two ways to track processed messages
Dedicated table: keep a PROCESSED_MESSAGES table whose primary key is (subscriberId, messageId). The consumer inserts the id inside its transaction; a duplicate delivery fails the INSERT on the primary-key constraint, so the handler rolls back and ignores the message. Embedded approach: store the message id inside the business entities the handler creates or updates, so the duplicate is detected by the domain data itself. Either way the database uniqueness constraint is what actually enforces exactly-once effect.

## Relation to exactly-once
The pattern does not promise exactly-once delivery from the broker (impossible). Instead it makes at-least-once delivery safe by guaranteeing exactly-once processing effect: applying the same message twice produces the same result as applying it once. Idempotent consumer plus transactional outbox is the canonical reliable-messaging pair for backend services.

title: Tyler Treat, You Cannot Have Exactly-Once Delivery (Brave New Geek)
text:
## The myth this debunks
A top backend engineer knows that 'exactly-once delivery' from a message system is a myth. Tyler Treat: in any distributed system, browser to server, server to database, or server to queue, 'you cannot have exactly-once message delivery.' Only two delivery semantics are actually feasible: at-most-once and at-least-once. Anyone selling exactly-once delivery is either redefining the term or hiding deduplication somewhere.

## Why it is impossible
The impossibility rests on two classic results. The Two Generals Problem: with an unreliable channel, one party can never be certain whether its message, or the acknowledgement of that message, was the thing that got lost, so no finite exchange of acks can guarantee agreement. The FLP result 'basically says, given the possibility of a faulty process, it is impossible for a system of processes to agree on a decision.' These are impossibility results, not just hard engineering.

## The acknowledgement dilemma
Everything reduces to when you acknowledge. Acknowledge before processing and you get at-most-once: if the receiver crashes mid-handling, the message is lost. Acknowledge after processing and you get at-least-once: if the receiver crashes before the ack reaches the sender, the sender retransmits and you get a duplicate. As Treat puts it: did the message get dropped, did the ack get dropped, or did the receiver crash? The sender cannot tell the difference, so it must retry, and retries create duplicates.

## The practical solution
Stop chasing exactly-once delivery; choose at-least-once and make your operations idempotent, so 'they can be applied more than once without adverse effects.' He cites Zab: applying the same state change multiple times does not cause inconsistency as long as the application order is consistent. Deduplication is the other option, but idempotency is the cleaner architecture. The engineering rule: design consumers so a redelivered message is a no-op, do not build systems that assume the broker will never redeliver.

title: AWS ElastiCache Documentation, Caching strategies (lazy loading, write-through, TTL)
text:
## Choosing a strategy depends on access pattern
AWS: which strategy you use to populate and maintain a cache depends on what data you cache and how it is accessed. A top-10 leaderboard and trending news stories need different strategies. The three canonical strategies are lazy loading, write-through, and adding TTL.

## Lazy loading (cache-aside)
Lazy loading loads data into the cache only when needed. On a read, the app asks the cache first. Cache hit: the cache returns the data. Cache miss: the cache returns null, the app queries the database, then the app writes the value back to the cache so the next read is fast. Advantages: only requested data is cached (most data is never requested, so you do not fill the cache with unused data), and node failures are not fatal (a new empty node just causes cache misses that repopulate it, with higher latency). Disadvantages: a cache-miss penalty of three trips (ask cache, query database, write cache), which adds noticeable delay; and stale data, because the cache is only written on a miss, so a database change is not reflected until the key expires or is evicted. This is the pattern usually called cache-aside.

## Write-through
Write-through adds or updates the cache every time data is written to the database. Advantages: data in the cache is never stale, because every database write also updates the cache; and the cost is a write penalty (two trips: write cache, write database) rather than a read penalty, which users tolerate better because updates feel like more work. Disadvantages: missing data, because a brand-new node has nothing until rows are next written (mitigate by combining write-through with lazy loading); and cache churn, because most data is never read, so writing everything through wastes cache space (mitigate with TTL).

## Adding TTL (the best of both)
Time to live (TTL) is an integer number of seconds until a key expires; when the app reads an expired key it is treated as not found, so the database is queried and the cache refreshed. Lazy loading tolerates stale data but never fails on empty nodes; write-through is always fresh but can fail on empty nodes and clutters the cache. Adding a TTL to each write gives you the advantages of both and largely avoids clutter: it does not guarantee a value is never stale, but it keeps data from getting too stale by forcing occasional refresh. The practical default: cache-aside reads plus a sensible TTL, and only add write-through for data that must never be stale. This is the concrete answer to 'cache invalidation is one of the two hard problems': prefer expiry (TTL) over trying to invalidate perfectly.

title: Stripe Engineering, Scaling your API with rate limiters (token bucket, load shedding)
text:
## Why rate limit
Rate limiting protects API availability by controlling traffic flow. Stripe added limiters for cases where one user causes a spike in traffic, or a user sends many lower-priority requests that could starve critical operations. A well-designed limiter keeps a single noisy client from degrading the service for everyone.

## The token bucket algorithm
Stripe uses the token bucket algorithm, implemented on Redis: a centralized bucket host holds tokens, each request takes a token, and tokens are slowly dripped back in over time. If the bucket is empty the request is rejected. The bucket size sets how large a short burst you tolerate; the drip rate sets the sustained allowed rate. This cleanly separates burst capacity from steady-state rate.

## Four layers of limiting and load shedding
1. Request rate limiter (most important): restricts each user to N requests per second, allowing brief bursts above the cap for real events like flash sales. This one rejected millions of requests in a month, largely runaway test-mode scripts. 2. Concurrent requests limiter: caps how many in-flight requests a user may have at once (for example 20), protecting CPU-heavy endpoints from users who retry and compound contention; triggered about 12,000 times a month. 3. Fleet usage load shedder: reserves a percentage of the fleet for critical methods (like charge creation) versus non-critical ones (like listing charges); non-critical requests over their allocation get a 503. 4. Worker utilization load shedder: the last line of defense in a major incident, sheds by priority in order, critical methods, then POST, then GET, then test-mode traffic, escalating gradually to avoid flapping.

## Practical rules
Return a clear 429 Too Many Requests (or 503 for load shedding) with an actionable message, hook limiters into middleware wrapped in exception handling so a limiter bug cannot take down the API, put a kill switch behind a feature flag, and dark-launch each limiter first (watch the traffic it would block before actually blocking). Prioritize critical business traffic over analytics or listing traffic when at capacity. Backpressure is not rudeness; a fast 429 is far kinder to clients than a slow timeout or a crashed service.

title: OWASP API Security Top 10, 2023 edition
text:
## Why a separate API Top 10
The OWASP API Security Top 10 is distinct from the general OWASP Top 10 because APIs have their own dominant failure modes, especially authorization at the object and function level. A backend engineer building services should treat this list as a checklist.

## The 2023 list
API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA): 'APIs tend to expose endpoints that handle object identifiers, creating a wide attack surface of Object Level Access Control issues.' The classic bug is /orders/{id} returning another user's order because the code loads by id but never checks ownership. This is the number-one API risk. API2:2023 Broken Authentication: authentication mechanisms are often implemented incorrectly, letting attackers compromise tokens or assume other identities. API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization: missing or improper authorization at the property level (mass assignment and excessive data exposure, for example letting a client set isAdmin, or returning fields the user should not see). API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption: no limits on requests, payload size, or expensive operations, leading to denial of service or runaway operational cost. API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization: complex access policies let attackers reach other users' resources or admin functions (for example a regular user calling an admin-only endpoint). API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows: exposing a business flow (checkout, ticket purchase) without defending against excessive automated use. API7:2023 Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF): the API fetches a remote resource from a user-supplied URI without validating it, letting an attacker reach internal services. API8:2023 Security Misconfiguration: insecure defaults, missing hardening, verbose errors. API9:2023 Improper Inventory Management: undocumented, deprecated, or shadow endpoints (old /v1, debug hosts) that expand the attack surface. API10:2023 Unsafe Consumption of APIs: trusting data from third-party APIs more than user input and applying weaker validation to it.

## The through-line
Most of these reduce to two backend disciplines: enforce authorization on every object and every function on the server for the authenticated principal (never trust an id or a role claim from the client), and put limits on everything (rate, size, depth, cost). Authentication tells you who; authorization must be checked per request per object.

title: OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet (secrets in code anti-pattern)
text:
## The anti-pattern: secrets in code
The common, dangerous practice is hardcoding secrets, API keys, database credentials, SSH keys, and certificates, in plaintext across source code, configuration files, and version control. Once a secret is committed it lives in git history forever, is copied to every clone and CI cache, and often leaks publicly. Secrets must never be hardcoded in source repositories or configuration management tools.

## Centralize and manage
Centralize the storage, provisioning, auditing, rotation, and management of secrets so you can control access and prevent leaks. Use a dedicated secrets manager or vault rather than scattering credentials. Document what each secret is for and where it lives.

## Encrypt everywhere
Protect secrets both at rest and in transit, using TLS for all transmissions. Store encryption keys separately from the secrets they protect (unless those keys are themselves encrypted).

## Least privilege and rotation
Apply least privilege rigorously: engineers should not have access to all secrets in the system; use fine-grained per-secret access policies. Automate rotation to minimize human handling. Prefer dynamic secrets that are generated when an application starts and invalidated on shutdown, which shrinks the window a leaked credential is useful.

## Do not log secrets, and detect commits
Mask or encrypt to avoid logging plaintext secrets during normal operation. Run secrets-detection tools in the development pipeline (pre-commit and CI scanning) to catch accidental commits before they reach version control. Maintain audit logs of who accessed which secret, when, and from where.

## When a secret leaks
Have a rapid revocation, rotation, and deletion procedure with clear escalation. The correct response to a leaked key is to rotate it, not to delete the commit: assume anything committed is already compromised. The backend rule: read secrets from the environment or a vault at runtime, keep them out of the repo, and make leaked-credential rotation a one-command operation.

title: Vlad Mihalcea, The N+1 query problem
text:
## Definition
The N+1 query problem, per Vlad Mihalcea (a recognized authority on data access performance), occurs when 'the data access framework executes N additional SQL statements to fetch the same data that could have been retrieved when executing the primary SQL query.' You run 1 query to load N parent rows, then 1 more query per parent to load its related child data, so you execute 1 + N queries instead of one. It is the single most common performance bug in ORM-backed backends.

## Concrete example
With a post and post_comment model: the inefficient path runs SELECT * FROM post_comment (1 query returning, say, 4 comments), then for each comment SELECT * FROM post WHERE id = ? (4 more queries), 5 total. The optimized path uses a single JOIN to fetch comments with their posts in one query. As N grows to hundreds or thousands, the naive version issues hundreds or thousands of round trips and falls over under load, while the joined version stays one query.

## Why it happens
In JPA/Hibernate the causes are: FetchType.EAGER defaults on @ManyToOne and @OneToOne, which force association fetches even when unnecessary; lazy-loaded associations accessed inside a loop, where touching the collection triggers a fresh query each iteration; and query caches that store only entity ids, requiring separate fetches. The same shape appears in any language: any loop that issues a query per element is an N+1. The give-away in logs is the identical parameterized SELECT repeated many times.

## Detection and fixes
Detect it by counting queries per request (assert on the count in tests) or watching the SQL log for a repeated single-row SELECT. Fix it by fetching all required data up front: use JOIN FETCH in JPQL or the Criteria API, or a single SQL query with a JOIN or a WHERE id IN (...) batch load, so N parents and their children come back together. Default associations to FetchType.LAZY so nothing is fetched implicitly, then explicitly join-fetch what a given use case needs. Second-level caching helps for hot entities. The rule: never query inside a loop, shape one query that returns exactly the rows the operation needs.

title: OWASP Mass Assignment Cheat Sheet (trusting client input anti-pattern)
text:
## The anti-pattern: blindly binding client input
Mass Assignment happens when a framework automatically binds HTTP request parameters to object fields, and the request can set fields the developer never intended. OWASP: 'Attackers can sometimes use this methodology to create new parameters that the developer never intended which in turn creates or overwrites new variable or objects in program code.' It is also called autobinding (Spring MVC, ASP.NET), object injection (PHP), or parameter binding. It is the concrete form of the general rule: never trust client input, and never map the request body straight onto your database model.

## Concrete example
A registration form legitimately has userid, password, email. The underlying User object also has an isAdmin boolean. The attacker simply adds the extra field: POST /addUser with userid=attacker&password=pass&email=test@example.com&isAdmin=true. A framework that binds every parameter sets isAdmin=true and grants admin. The 2012 GitHub breach was exactly this: a user uploaded a public key to any organization and could make subsequent changes to their repositories.

## Mitigations
Allow-listing (recommended): explicitly list the fields that may be bound, for example Spring binder.setAllowedFields([userid, password, email]) or Laravel protected $fillable = [userid, password, email]. Block-listing: protect sensitive fields, for example binder.setDisallowedFields([isAdmin]) or Laravel $guarded = [isAdmin]; weaker because it fails open when a new sensitive field is added. Data Transfer Objects (DTOs): accept a dedicated input class that contains only the editable fields, then map it explicitly onto the domain or database entity, so protected fields like isAdmin, balance, role, or ownerId can never be set from the request. The backend discipline: validate and bind through an explicit schema (a Zod schema, a DTO, a serializer), assign server-controlled fields (owner, timestamps, roles) on the server, and treat any field the client should not control as forbidden by default.

title: Eric Brewer, CAP Twelve Years Later: How the Rules Have Changed (InfoQ)
text:
## The three properties
Eric Brewer, who stated the CAP theorem, defines three properties of a networked shared-data system. Consistency (C): 'equivalent to having a single up-to-date copy of the data.' Availability (A): 'of that data (for updates).' Partition tolerance (P): the ability to keep operating despite network partitions between components. The theorem: 'any networked shared-data system can have at most two of three desirable properties.'

## Why the popular '2 of 3' reading is wrong
Brewer says 'the two of three view is misleading on several fronts.' First, partitions are rare, 'because partitions are rare, there is little reason to forfeit C or A when the system is not partitioned,' so in normal operation you get both C and A. Second, the choice between C and A is fine-grained: 'the choice between C and A can occur many times within the same system at very fine granularity; not only can subsystems make different choices, but the choice can change according to the operation or even the specific data or user involved.' Third, all three properties are more continuous than binary: availability ranges from 0 to 100 percent, there are many consistency levels, and partitions have nuances. You do not statically pick two; you decide per operation, and only when a partition actually occurs.

## The real dynamic: the partition decision
'Operationally, the essence of CAP takes place during a timeout, a period when the program must make a fundamental decision, the partition decision: cancel the operation and thus decrease availability, or proceed with the operation and thus risk inconsistency.' So CAP is not a permanent architecture label (calling a database 'CP' or 'AP' is itself an oversimplification); it is a runtime choice made during partitions.

## Managing partitions in three steps
Brewer proposes explicit partition management: detect the start of a partition, enter a partition mode that limits certain operations, and then initiate recovery, restoring consistency and compensating for mistakes made during the partition. The backend takeaway: understand that during a network partition you must consciously trade availability against consistency, choose per operation (a 'like' can proceed optimistically, a payment cannot), and plan the reconciliation/recovery path rather than pretending partitions never happen. Eventual consistency is the deliberate choice to favor availability during partitions and reconcile afterward.

title: PgBouncer Documentation, Features (connection pooling modes)
text:
## Why pool connections
PgBouncer is a lightweight connection pooler for PostgreSQL. It matters because each direct PostgreSQL connection is backed by a separate server process with its own memory, so opening thousands of connections (for example one per serverless request or a large app-server pool) exhausts the database. PgBouncer sits in front and multiplexes many client connections onto a small set of real server connections; it needs only about 2 kB per connection, so it holds many idle clients cheaply while keeping the expensive database backends few and busy.

## Three pooling modes
Session pooling (most conservative): when a client connects, a server connection is assigned to it for the whole duration it stays connected. It supports all PostgreSQL features without limitation, but a client that holds an idle connection ties up a backend. Transaction pooling (the common high-throughput choice): a server connection is assigned to a client only during a transaction, and is returned to the pool between transactions, so far fewer server connections serve many clients. The cost: it breaks session-based features and needs the application to cooperate. Statement pooling (most aggressive): transaction pooling with the twist that multi-statement transactions are disallowed, enforcing autocommit at the client.

## Transaction pooling limitations
Transaction pooling does not support session-level features because a client does not keep the same backend across statements: SET and RESET, LISTEN/NOTIFY, WITH HOLD cursors, PREPARE/DEALLOCATE style prepared statements, LOAD, and session-level advisory locks are not safe. If you use transaction pooling you must avoid these or scope them within a single transaction. This is why frameworks and poolers must be configured together: a transaction-pooled connection is not a stable session, so per-session state and server-side prepared statements can silently break. The backend rule: size the pool to the database's real capacity, prefer transaction pooling for high connection counts, and design the app to not rely on session state that pooling cannot preserve.

title: oauth.net, OAuth 2.0 (authorization framework overview)
text:
## What OAuth 2.0 is
'OAuth 2.0 is the industry-standard protocol for authorization.' It emphasizes client developer simplicity while providing specific authorization flows for web applications, desktop applications, mobile phones, and devices. It is defined by RFC 6749 and a family of related RFCs.

## The four roles
RFC 6749 defines the interaction between four roles: the resource owner (the user who owns the data), the client (the application requesting access), the authorization server (issues tokens after authenticating the resource owner and getting consent), and the resource server (the API that holds the protected resources and accepts access tokens). The point of OAuth is that the client obtains restricted access on behalf of the user without ever handling the user's password.

## Tokens
The authorization server issues an access token that grants constrained, time-limited permissions (scopes) so the client can call the resource server on the user's behalf. A refresh token lets the client obtain new access tokens without forcing the user to re-authenticate. Access tokens should be treated as bearer credentials: whoever holds one can use it, so transmit them only over TLS, keep their lifetime short, and scope them narrowly.

## Grant types (flows)
The main flows: Authorization Code, with PKCE for enhanced security (the recommended flow for web, mobile, and single-page apps); Client Credentials (for machine-to-machine, no user involved); Device Code (for input-constrained devices); and Refresh Token. The legacy Implicit and Resource Owner Password Credentials (password grant) flows are deprecated and should not be used in new systems.

## Authorization, not authentication
Critically, OAuth 2.0 handles authorization only, deciding what a client may access. It does not by itself tell you who the user is in a reliable way. OpenID Connect is a separate protocol built on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds the authentication layer (an ID token identifying the user). The common backend mistake is using a raw OAuth access token as proof of identity; use OpenID Connect for login, OAuth 2.0 for delegated API access.

title: Microsoft Learn, Database normalization description (1NF, 2NF, 3NF)
text:
## What normalization is and why
Normalization is the process of organizing data in a relational database: creating tables and relationships according to rules that protect the data and make the schema flexible by eliminating redundancy and inconsistent dependency. Redundant data wastes disk space and creates maintenance problems: if the same fact lives in several places, every copy must be changed identically on an update, or the data goes inconsistent. Storing a customer's address only in the Customers table means an address change happens in exactly one place. An inconsistent dependency is data placed where its access path does not naturally lead (an employee's salary does not belong in the Customers table). The rules are called normal forms; observing the first three gives third normal form, considered the highest level necessary for most applications.

## First normal form (1NF)
Eliminate repeating groups in individual tables; create a separate table for each set of related data; identify each set with a primary key. Do not use multiple fields (Class1, Class2, Class3, or Vendor Code 1, Vendor Code 2) to store similar data, because that cannot accommodate a dynamic number of values. Instead move the repeating group into its own table linked by a key. A one-to-many relationship must not put the one side and the many side in the same row.

## Second normal form (2NF)
Create separate tables for sets of values that apply to multiple records and relate them with a foreign key. Records should not depend on anything other than the table's primary key (a compound key if necessary). In the student example, Class# is not functionally dependent on Student# alone, so classes move to a separate Registration table, leaving Students keyed only by Student#.

## Third normal form (3NF)
Eliminate fields that do not depend on the key. Values in a record that are not part of that record's key do not belong in the table. In the student example Adv-Room (the advisor's office) depends on the Advisor, not on the Student, so it moves to a Faculty table keyed by advisor. If a group of fields could apply to more than one record, put them in their own table.

## The practical caveat
Perfect third normal form is not always practical: splitting out cities, ZIP codes, and every duplicable factor produces many small tables that can degrade performance. A reasonable rule is to apply 3NF especially to data that changes frequently, and denormalize deliberately (with eyes open to the redundancy you are accepting) only where measured performance demands it. Fourth normal form (BCNF) and fifth normal form exist but are rarely needed in practical design. The engineering judgment: normalize by default to avoid update anomalies, denormalize as a considered optimization, never by accident.

title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Chatty I/O antipattern
text:
## The anti-pattern
Chatty I/O is when the cumulative effect of a large number of small I/O requests significantly hurts performance and responsiveness. Network calls and I/O are inherently slow compared to compute, and each request carries significant overhead (connection setup, round-trip latency, per-request processing), so many small requests add up. Common causes: reading and writing individual database records as distinct requests (an O/RM can mask this as the N+1 problem where child records are fetched one at a time), implementing one logical operation as a series of fine-grained HTTP requests, and repeatedly opening/writing/closing a file for small writes.

## The chatty web API
A classic example exposes each property of a User through its own HTTP GET (/users/{id}/username, /users/{id}/gender, /users/{id}/dateofbirth). Nothing is technically wrong, but a client that needs several properties must make several round trips. This often happens when developers treat remote objects like local in-memory objects. The fix: follow REST design and return the whole User from one GET /users/{id}, a larger response body but far fewer calls.

## How to fix
Reduce the number of I/O requests by packaging data into larger, fewer requests. Fetch related database data in a single query (for example Entity Framework Include of Product.ProductListPriceHistory) instead of a query per child. Buffer file writes in memory and write once. Follow coarser-grained (chunky) API operations that return related data together.

## The measured impact
In the sample, the chatty GetProductsInSubCategoryAsync performed 45 SELECT queries, each opening a new SQL connection, and at 1,000 users median response time was nearly a minute, sustaining about 410 requests per minute. Rewriting it as a single joined query dropped average response time at 1,000 users to about 5 to 6 seconds and raised throughput to about 3,970 requests per minute. Complex joins can be expensive, but relational databases are optimized for exactly that kind of query, and it runs once per operation.

## The balance with over-fetching
Fewer, larger calls trade against fetching data you do not need. The right granularity depends on real usage: if clients usually need only the username, a dedicated endpoint may be justified. Detect chatty I/O by monitoring for high latency and low throughput, then load-test and trace: a large number of small requests to the same file, service, or data store, and applications becoming I/O bound, are the tells.

title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Extraneous Fetching antipattern (over-fetching, SELECT *)
text:
## The anti-pattern
Extraneous fetching is retrieving more data than a business operation needs, causing unnecessary I/O overhead and reduced responsiveness. It often appears as overcompensation for chatty I/O (grabbing everything you might need in one shot) or from poor design: fetching all rows/columns and then filtering or aggregating in application memory. The two smells are too many columns (a poorly designed SELECT * that pulls fields nobody uses) and too many rows (missing WHERE filtering, unbounded queries).

## Concrete examples
Fetching every product with all columns then projecting to just Id and Name in memory: the projection should be part of the query. Computing total sales by loading every order's TotalDue into the app and summing in memory: the SUM should run in the database. A subtle Entity Framework case: calling AsEnumerable (or using a method LINQ cannot translate, like DateTime.AddDays inside the where) forces filtering onto the client side over IEnumerable, so every Product row is returned and filtered in memory instead of the database. IQueryable pushes filtering to the data source; IEnumerable does not.

## How to fix
Only fetch the data the operation needs. Select just the required columns as part of the query, not after. Run aggregations in the database (SumAsync) rather than in application memory. Keep LINQ resolving over IQueryable so predicates reach the database; factor out untranslatable expressions (compute dateSince = Now.AddDays(-7) first, then compare in the query). For unbounded queries, paginate and fetch a limited number of entities at a time. Use WHERE clauses and built-in aggregate functions. Caveat: do not offload work to a database that is not optimized for it (the Busy Database antipattern is the opposite failure).

## The measured impact
For GetAllFieldsAsync the database returned 80,503 bytes per request but the client response was only 19,855 bytes, about 25 percent, so three quarters of the transferred data was wasted. The client-side aggregation was more extreme: over 280 KB pulled from the database to produce a 14-byte JSON number. After projecting only needed fields, response time at 400 users fell from about 4 seconds to about 1.3 seconds and throughput rose from about 100 to 350 requests per second. Moving the aggregation into the database cut per-transaction data from over 280 KB to 53 bytes and raised sustained throughput from around 2,000 to over 25,000 requests per minute. The rule: select only the columns and rows you use, and filter and aggregate in the query, not in the app.
